blocks.text: Neonatal jaundice is yellow discoloration of the skin and sclera resulting from elevated serum bilirubin.

rows: Maternal antibodies destroy neonatal red cells

items.text: Early jaundice: Within the first 24 hours — always pathological until proven otherwise.
Physiological jaundice: Usually appears after 24 hours.
Prolonged jaundice: Persists beyond the expected period, requiring investigation.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise. Always fractionate bilirubin when evaluating prolonged jaundice or suspected cholestasis.

items.text: Rapid bilirubin rise, particularly ≥0.3 mg/dL/hour in the first 24 hours or ≥0.2 mg/dL/hour thereafter.
A bilirubin level exceeding the age-, gestation- and risk-specific treatment threshold.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Do not use one universal bilirubin threshold for all newborns. Treatment depends on postnatal age in hours, gestational age and neurotoxicity risk factors.
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia suggests impaired bile formation or bile flow and is always pathological in a neonate.

rows: Infections, including neonatal sepsis and CMV

items.text: Endocrine disorders, including hypothyroidism and hypopituitarism.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: A jaundiced infant with pale stools and dark urine should raise immediate suspicion of biliary atresia. Urgent specialist assessment is essential because early surgical intervention improves outcomes.

rows: Sickle cell disease and other red-cell disorders

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood-brain barrier and cause bilirubin encephalopathy. Conjugated bilirubin does not cause kernicterus in the same way.

items.text: Iatrogenic blood loss from repeated sampling.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Anaemia at birth suggests blood loss, haemolysis or impaired fetal erythropoiesis. Anaemia of prematurity typically develops later.

items.text: Coagulase-negative staphylococci, especially in hospital-acquired infection.

rows: Staphylococci, Klebsiella, E. coli and other hospital/community organisms

items.text: R – Rupture of membranes for prolonged periods.
R – Risk factors such as maternal GBS colonisation.

blocks.text: Other risks include invasive procedures, central venous catheters and prolonged hospitalisation.
Exam pearl: Neonatal sepsis may present with hypothermia rather than fever. A normal temperature does not exclude infection.
Neonatal seizures are abnormal neurological events occurring in the neonatal period. They may be subtle and difficult to recognise.

rows: Inborn errors of metabolism and other metabolic disorders

items.text: L – Limb cycling or repetitive movements.
Blood culture when infection is suspected.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Clinical observation alone may not reliably distinguish neonatal seizures from non-epileptic movements. EEG is important for confirmation.
Respiratory distress in a newborn is characterised by increased work of breathing.

rows: Extrapulmonary causes, such as congenital heart disease

items.text: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn.

rows: Respiratory distress syndrome, congenital anomalies, aspiration

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Respiratory rate above 60 breaths/minute in a newborn is tachypnoea. Always assess oxygenation and work of breathing, not respiratory rate alone.
Cyanosis is a bluish discoloration resulting from increased deoxygenated haemoglobin or abnormal haemoglobin pigments.

rows: Bluish hands and feet, with relatively pink tongue

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: Acrocyanosis can be normal in the immediate newborn period, but central cyanosis is always concerning.

items.text: I – Infant of a diabetic mother.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: An at-risk newborn may have hypoglycaemia without symptoms. Follow local screening and treatment protocols; do not wait for symptoms before checking glucose in a high-risk infant.

rows: Open incubator or inadequate thermal protection

items.text: R – Rapidly dry and remove wet towels.
M – Maintain skin-to-skin contact or appropriate thermal care.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Premature and low-birth-weight babies are particularly vulnerable to heat loss because of their large surface-area-to-weight ratio and immature thermoregulation.

rows: Heat exposure and excessive environmental warming

items.text: Environmental overheating: The infant may be hot because of excessive external heat.
Fever: May indicate an underlying infectious or inflammatory process.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: A temperature of 38°C or higher in a neonate requires urgent assessment for serious infection, even when environmental overheating is suspected.

rows: Excessive anticoagulant exposure or maternal medications

blocks.text: Classification of vitamin K deficiency bleeding
Exam pearl: Vitamin K deficiency classically causes prolonged PT/INR, often with prolonged aPTT in more severe deficiency, while platelet count is generally normal.

Birth asphyxia is a historical clinical term associated with failure to establish adequate breathing at birth and possible impairment of oxygen delivery. Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE) describes neurological injury resulting from impaired oxygen and blood supply.

rows: Young gestational age and prematurity-related vulnerability

blocks.text: Important distinction: A low Apgar score alone does not establish intrapartum asphyxia or predict an individual infant's long-term neurological outcome.
Exam pearl: Neonatal resuscitation prioritises effective ventilation. Persistent bradycardia in a newborn is commonly due to inadequate lung inflation and oxygenation.
Exam pearl: The lower the gestational age, generally the greater the risk of complications associated with prematurity.

rows: Hyperalert, irritable, increased muscle tone, usually no seizures
Stupor or coma, flaccidity, absent reflexes, severe EEG abnormalities

blocks.text: Therapeutic hypothermia is used in appropriately selected term or near-term infants with moderate-to-severe HIE, generally initiated within 6 hours of birth and continued for 72 hours under specialist neonatal protocols.
Exam pearl: Therapeutic hypothermia is a controlled medical intervention. It must not be confused with accidental neonatal hypothermia.
Chronic bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction resulting from bilirubin deposition in vulnerable brain structures, particularly the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei.
Exam pearl: Early recognition and treatment of severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia prevent bilirubin-induced neurological injury.
Mnemonic: WARM → ASSESS → VENTILATE → COMPRESS → MEDICATE
Neonatal resuscitation focuses on establishing effective ventilation and circulation immediately after birth.

items.text: Does the baby have good tone?
Is the baby breathing or crying?

blocks.text: If all are yes, provide routine newborn care.
If no, proceed to initial stabilisation.

items.text: A – Align the airway in a neutral or slightly extended position.
R – Remove wet linen and dry.

blocks.text: Suction only when needed, such as suspected airway obstruction.

content_groups.group_title: Step 3: Assess breathing and heart rate

items.text: Apnoea or gasping: Start positive-pressure ventilation.
Heart rate below 100/minute: Start or continue effective ventilation.
Heart rate at least 100/minute: Assess respiratory effort and support as required.

blocks.text: If the newborn is apnoeic, gasping or has a heart rate below 100/minute despite initial steps, provide effective positive-pressure ventilation.
Reassess chest movement and heart rate.
If the heart rate remains below 60/minute after at least 30 seconds of effective ventilation that inflates the lungs, start coordinated chest compressions.

items.text: Approximately 90 compressions and 30 ventilations per minute.

blocks.title: If heart rate remains below 60/minute despite effective ventilation and coordinated compressions:

items.text: Give adrenaline according to neonatal resuscitation guidelines.
Consider volume expansion if blood loss or hypovolaemia is suspected.

rows: After approximately 60 seconds of coordinated compressions and ventilation

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Effective ventilation is the single most important intervention in neonatal resuscitation. Do not delay ventilation to perform prolonged suctioning or other non-essential procedures.
APGAR is used to assess the newborn's condition at 1 and 5 minutes after birth, and subsequently when indicated.

items.text: Repeat every 5 minutes up to 20 minutes if the score remains below 7.
Prematurity and maternal medications may influence the score.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Never wait for an APGAR score before initiating resuscitation. Resuscitation is guided by breathing and heart rate, not the APGAR score.
The New Ballard Score estimates gestational age by assessing physical and neuromuscular maturity.
Mnemonic: POSTURE ARM SQUARE WINDOW SCARF HEEL

rows: Return of arm to flexed position
Resistance when arm is moved across chest
Resistance when heel is moved towards ear

blocks.text: Mnemonic: SKIN LANUGO PLANTAR BREAST EYE GENITALIA

rows: Testicular descent and scrotal appearance in males; labial development in females

blocks.text: The scores from all six neuromuscular and six physical parameters are combined to estimate gestational age.
The New Ballard Score generally estimates gestational age from approximately 20 to 44 weeks.
Exam pearl: Ballard scoring is particularly useful when the maternal dates are uncertain, but its accuracy may be affected by severe illness, neurological depression and growth restriction.
This is an expanded examination of the New Ballard Score, which is particularly important for practical and OSCE assessments.

items.text: Ensure the baby is warm and clinically stable.
Examine skin, lanugo and plantar creases.
Examine breast tissue, eyes, ears and genitalia.
Calculate the total score and estimate gestational age using the New Ballard conversion chart.
APGAR assesses immediate adaptation after birth.
Ballard assesses physical and neuromuscular maturity.
Neither replaces accurate obstetric dating when reliable early pregnancy ultrasound is available.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Do not confuse the Ballard score with the Dubowitz assessment. They are different methods of estimating gestational age.
Mnemonic: ROOT – SUCK – MORO – GRASP – STEP
Neonatal primitive reflexes are involuntary responses present at birth. They help assess neurological integrity and maturation.

rows: Turns towards stimulus and opens mouth
Sudden controlled change in head support
Arm extension and abduction followed by flexion
Hold upright with feet touching surface
Extension of face-side limbs and flexion of opposite limbs
Great toe extends and other toes fan

blocks.text: These are approximate ages; normal variation occurs.

items.text: Sudden extension and abduction of arms.
Opens mouth to seek the nipple.
Absent Moro reflex bilaterally: May indicate neurological depression or severe illness.
Unilateral absent Moro: Consider clavicular fracture, brachial plexus injury or local pain.
Persistent primitive reflexes: May suggest neurological dysfunction.
Asymmetric reflexes: Consider focal neurological or musculoskeletal pathology.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: The plantar response may be extensor in a normal infant because corticospinal tract maturation is incomplete. This does not automatically indicate an upper motor neuron lesion.
Neonatal sepsis risk factors can be divided into maternal, intrapartum and neonatal factors.

rows: Organism colonisation, especially Group B Streptococcus
History of previous infant with GBS disease

items.text: Inadequate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis when indicated.
Maternal HIV infection, depending on exposure and prevention measures.

rows: Young gestational age and low birth weight

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Maternal risk factors help assess early-onset neonatal sepsis, while invasive procedures and prolonged hospitalisation are particularly important in late-onset sepsis.
Phototherapy is used to reduce unconjugated bilirubin in newborns by converting bilirubin into water-soluble photoisomers that can be excreted without hepatic conjugation.

rows: Levels of bilirubin exceed the treatment threshold
Increased haemolysis with rapidly rising bilirubin
Treatment guided by postnatal age in hours

items.text: Total serum bilirubin reaches or exceeds the applicable phototherapy threshold.
Rapidly rising bilirubin, especially with suspected haemolysis, when it approaches treatment thresholds.
Selected infants with significant risk of bilirubin neurotoxicity.
Protect the eyes according to the equipment and protocol.
Bronze baby syndrome, particularly in conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Phototherapy thresholds must be obtained from an appropriate gestational-age- and hour-specific guideline chart. Do not use a single bilirubin concentration for every newborn.

Exchange transfusion is a procedure in which the infant's blood is progressively removed and replaced with compatible donor blood to rapidly reduce bilirubin and remove circulating antibodies and sensitised red cells.

rows: Clinical features of acute bilirubin encephalopathy
Greatly elevated bilirubin despite intensive phototherapy

items.text: Total serum bilirubin reaches the exchange transfusion threshold.
Severe haemolytic disease with bilirubin rising despite intensive phototherapy.
Severe hyperbilirubinaemia associated with high risk of neurological injury.

rows: Removes bilirubin and antibody-coated red cells
Used when exchange threshold is reached or neurological signs develop

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Continue intensive phototherapy while preparing for exchange transfusion. Do not delay exchange transfusion in a baby with signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
